en: Abhinanda: May the strides of Śauri, which were equally laborious in both cases, bestow prosperity upon you—those which first traversed the footprint of a cow and those which subsequently traversed the three worlds. (AKad 1.1)
The eloquent words of my father Jayanta, the teacher of the world—words full of aesthetic flavor, adorned with ornaments, and sweet in their clarity—triumph. AKad_1.2 //
For virtuous people who are lamps illuminating excellence, there is nothing more radiant than even their defiled actions, for these serve as an adornment for the vision of others.
Virtue expands even when it is slight, while vice diminishes even when it is vast;
having encountered the virtuous and the wicked, it becomes like the bright and dark fortnights of the moon.
There was a Gauḍa Brahmin named Śakti in the lineage of Bhāradvāja;
having reached Dārvābhisāra, he took a wife.
He had a son named Mitra, a treasury of splendors,
whose rising was honored by the people who were awakened to the cessation of faults.
He obtained as his son Śaktisvāmin, who was renowned for his learning and served as the minister of King Muktāpīḍa of the Karkoṭa dynasty.
To this Kalyāṇasvāmin was born a son named Āryaśūra, who— like Yājñavalkya— had shaken off the defilements of worldly existence through the power of pure yoga.
From that man of unfathomable heart was born a beloved son, the ornament of the Supreme Lord, like the moon born from the ocean of milk.
He begot a son named Jayanta, who brought joy to the people;
his eloquence bore fruit in both poetry and oratory.
He who clearly bore the second name Vṛttikāra was a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and an expounder of the meaning of all treatises.
From him was born a wise son named Jayanta, who was a knower of the principles of excellent literature; from him, in turn, arose the one renowned as Abhinanda.
For those whose intellects are weary from the labor of composing extensive poetry,
he has therefore extracted merely the narrative from the ocean of the *Kādambarī*.
On the bank of the Vetravatī river stood a city named Vidiśā, an ornament of the earth whose splendor rivaled that of Indra’s city.
It shone like the very abode of heaven for those of meritorious deeds and radiant splendor,
with the lattices of light from its jeweled houses possessing the brilliance of Indra’s bow.
In that city there was a glorious king named Śūdraka, who, like Ākhaṇḍala (Indra), had conquered the circle of his enemies through the exertion of his own arms. (A pair) AKad_1.16 //
Though he assumed the forms of the eight world-protectors,
he was known as the Moon because he constantly delighted living beings with them.
*Yugmam* (A pair):
Having completely conquered the earth girt by the four oceans,
he dwelt there at his ease, having entrusted the burden of governance to his ministers.
Thus, during his youth, he passed his days with diversions that did not disturb the people and were not inconsistent with wealth and virtue.
And his mind, which had seen the further shore of those pleasures unattainable by others, turned away from the amorous play of youth, even though he was still young.
Even with great effort, that woman could not, by means of the god whose arrows are flowers,
win over his heart or even his eye.
Then, on one occasion, a female door-keeper, having approached him as he was staying in the outer courtyard, bowed low with affection and addressed him thus: AKad_1.22.
Having brought from afar the parrot of wondrous behavior as a gift, a certain Caṇḍāla girl arrived, desiring an audience. (AK 1.23)
Having heard this, the king reflected for a moment, looked at the faces of his ministers, and commanded her: "What is the harm? Let her enter."
Then, avoiding contact with the world by means of her own mark,
the daughter of a Mātaṅga entered the king’s courtyard, having been granted permission.
And together with her, an old Caṇḍāla entered, carrying a golden cage containing a parrot in his hand and maintaining an appearance of harmlessness.
But seeing that maiden of wondrous appearance as she entered, the king was greatly amazed and reflected thus for a moment: AKad_1.27 //
This form, this radiance, these sprays of loveliness—
these do not even indicate the state of being mortal, let alone the state of being an elephant.
I see this as nothing but the truth: surely some deity, concealed by the illusory power (*māyā*) of a *mātaṅga*, has descended into the world of mortals.
As he was reflecting in this way, she, looking upon him with an untroubled gaze, bowed to the protector of the earth like a woman of bold character.

Then, with his knees placed upon the ground and his neck bowed, the old man, holding the cage firmly with both hands, said: ||| AKad_31 ||| The old man, with his knees pressed against the surface of the earth and his neck bent low, spoke while holding the cage tightly with both hands. ||| AKad_31 |||
This parrot named Vaiśampāyana is a most wonderful jewel;
he is a deity who is the very abode of jewels, like another ocean of milk.
"Thus has this bird been brought to us with great devotion by our mistress’s daughter; please show her favor and accept the bird."
Having spoken thus, he placed the cage before the king upon the jeweled floor, bowed respectfully to him, and withdrew.
The female doorkeeper, perceiving his intention, opened the panels of the door; she opened the cage, and the bird flew out from it.
Lifting his right foot and uttering the word "Victory," he, having applied Vedic mantras and blessings, then recited this noble verse: AKad_1.36.
The pair of breasts of your enemies' wives, bathed in tears and situated close to the fire of grief in their hearts,
moves about without ornaments as if performing a vow of penance.
Having heard this, the protector of the earth, his eyes wide with wonder,
spoke to his chief minister named Kumārapāla.
Have you ever seen or even heard of such a marvel?
What kind of excellence is this in the state of an animal that is so difficult to find among humans?
The refinement of learning and study, association with the Mātaṅga people,
and this maiden among the Mātaṅgas— this is a succession of wonders.
But the minister replied: "O Lord, extraordinary qualities generally arise in living beings due to the influence of past conditioning; what is there to wonder at in this?"
These very marks are established by logicians as the grounds for inferring the existence of the next world, in order to refute the materialists (Lokāyatikas).
The creation of the Creator is diverse; the latent impressions of karma are diverse;
their maturation is diverse; and the succession of time is diverse.
At that moment, the sound of the midday drum arose, loud and deep, causing the interruption of this narrative concerning Śuka.
Let comfortable dwellings and the like be prepared for her outside;
meanwhile, let this king of birds be ushered inside.
Having thus instructed the female door-keeper, the lord of the earth left the assembly hall and dismissed the circle of kings who had come for the purpose of service.
Then, having performed some light exercise, bathed, worshipped the deities,
offered oblations into the fire, and received the blessings of learned brahmins, he ate his meal and went to his bedchamber.
There, having ascended his couch and meditated for a brief moment,
he summoned Śuka once again as he rested in the inner apartments.
Having first inquired about his well-being from the chamberlain who had brought him,
he, drawn by curiosity, immediately asked for an account of his adventures.
"Vaiśampāyana, who are you? Where were you born? Where have you lived for so long?
From where does such proficiency in the arts, sciences, and other branches of knowledge as this come to you?"
I think you must be someone who remembers his former births, having come to this earth;
for such a degree of excellence as this does not exist among the species of birds.
Or by whom was this name, befitting a brahmin, given to you? From where do such names come from in the houses of the low-born?
"How did you come into contact with a caṇḍāla here, or how did you arrive?"— you ought to tell me your entire story in full.
Thus questioned by the lord of the earth with great respect,
Śuka reflected for a moment with his intellect and began to speak.
O King, the Vindhya forest, which reaches from the shores of the eastern to those of the western ocean, has now come within the range of your hearing.
When Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, together with Sītā, dwelt in the Daṇḍaka forest, where trees were torn down by elephants whose temples were itchy in certain spots; AKad_1.56.
*A pair:* There stood the hermitage of the sage Agastya, esteemed by the self-controlled,
where the trees were nourished by the water poured from the hands of Lopāmudrā.
In its vicinity lies a lake of meritorious waters called Pampā,
where Sītā plucked an ear-ornament lotus with the palm of her hand.
On its western bank there is an ancient śālmali tree,
whose height and circumference pervade the intermediate space between the sky and the quarters of the world.
In that inaccessible place, thousands of birds dwell continuously, free from fear, having built their nests there.
Having secured their sustenance here and there during the day,
they return there to their own nests and sleep happily through the nights.
My parents remained settled right there;
I was born as their only son during the latter part of their lives.
Unable to endure the intense pains of childbirth,
she brought about my own mother’s death, that very woman who bore me, wretched as I am.
Although my father was consumed by the pain of separation from his wife and distressed by his longing for a son,
he cast aside his grief and applied himself with effort to nourishing my life.
Unable to go anywhere for the sake of his own livelihood,
he remained day and night right there in the nest, holding me against his chest.
He sustained himself with fruits and other food brought by others on leaf-plates, which had been eaten and then discarded,
and which remained after he had satisfied his hunger.
Then, as time passed and my wings had slightly begun to sprout,
I became eager to fly, even though I remained upon my father’s chest.
Suddenly,
a tumultuous clamor, like the drum of Yama, arose in that forest, causing the flocks of beasts and birds to flee in terror.
Then, slightly raising my neck from my chest,
I cast my eyes in all directions out of curiosity.
Then I saw a leader of the Śabara tribes coming through the forest, surrounded by an innumerable retinue of Kirātas, out of a passion for the hunt.
Then, out of fear, I thought of myself as if dead, like a *śālmali* tree uprooted, and like a forest turned upside down.
In an instant, that forest was then filled with those hunters, who were smeared with the blood flowing from the limbs of thousands of slaughtered creatures.
Then that sword-wielding general, weary from the exertions of the hunt,
sat down upon the grassy bank of Lake Pampā.
Having rested for a moment, drunk water, and eaten young lotus stalks,
the commander-in-chief departed with the Pulindas by the same way he had come.
But there hung a single wicked old Pulinda,
tall and of terrifying appearance, like a servant of the God of Death.
Having experienced his efforts in vain and failing to obtain even a piece of raw flesh,
he cast his gaze upon that śālmali tree as if it were a messenger of Yama.
Although he knew that great tree was difficult to climb and,
though his resolve had already been born, he nevertheless made an effort to ascend it.
Then, my mind overwhelmed by incomparable terror,
I entered my father’s lap, my body covered by his wings.
But that wicked man, having climbed that tree,
killed the parrots dwelling in the nest again and again as much as he was able, and threw them to the ground.
In due course, that man of evil conduct broke his father’s neck as well and cast him, deprived of life, upon the ground.
At that time, I had no grief for him nor anything else in my mind;
I was overwhelmed solely by a natural fear.
Then, emerging from my father's lap with trepidation,
I quickly entered the hollow among the withered leaves of the trees.
Then that wicked man, having descended from the base of the śālmali tree and taken the lifeless parrots, went away in pursuit of the hunters.
But because I had the color of withered leaves at that time, I was not recognized by that evildoer due to the decree of fate.
Then, when that cruel deed had been carried out far away,
thirst oppressed me as hope for life had arisen within me.
Lacking the power to fly,
being thirsty, I desired to go as best I could on foot along the banks of the Pampā lake.
Nevertheless, utterly disheartened, he falls again and again here and there,
suspecting that very evildoer at every step.
Lamenting for a long time, "Alas, father! Father!", I remained there, exceedingly cruel, while my life-breaths, lingering at the very throat, were being exhausted.
Not very far from that lake is the hermitage of the sage Jābāli, a treasury of asceticism who has shaken off the entire web of afflictions. *Yugmam* (This concludes the pair of verses).
Then his son, named Hārīta, came to that lake to bathe and beheld me there in that condition.
"Alas! By some misfortune this young parrot has been cast down from its nest and is suffering," he said, and out of compassion he took me by the hand.
He repeatedly made the drops of milk flow for him while soothing the horse;
and having performed his daily rites, out of compassion he led him to his father’s hermitage.
As I beheld Hārītī’s father with my very eyes, my heart, now comforted, felt as if a firm foothold had been placed within it by the hope of life.
"This young bird, fallen from its nest, has been brought by me," he said,
bowing to his father and showing him me held in his hand.
Then I beheld Jābāli, appearing like the Grandfather [Brahmā] in person,
surrounded by high-souled ascetics rich in austerity who were full of compassion.
With hair white with old age, his bodily limbs and form were barely discernible due to the radiance spreading outward from him.
But he, having gazed at me for a moment as if smiling, said:
"For this fruit of one's own very action is what is being experienced by this [being]."
For that Blessed One, who perceives the three times, beholds the universe with his divine eye as clearly as a jujube or an emblic myrobalan fruit held in the palm of his hand.
Having heard those words, all the sages, agitated by curiosity, gathered together and said to him:
"O Blessed One, who was this person in a previous existence, and what was his evil conduct? Let that be told."
Thus entreated and urged by the sages, he said to them: "Perform first your own daily rites;
then, having completed the evening ritual with unerring attention, you shall hear his extensive story."
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, the sages spent their day according to their own respective routines of practice;
and I too passed the remainder of the day with various mental diversions provided by Hārīta’s hands.
Thus ends the first canto in the *Kādambarī-kathāsāra*, the work of Abhinanda, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Jayanta, who was among the foremost of the most excellent of the wise.
The Second Canto:
Then, having completed their ritual duties up to the conclusion of the twilight devotions, the sages—
Desirous of hearing, they gathered together and sat down according to their respective places.
I too, eager to hear the details of my own life story,
then restrained all my restlessness and remained with a steady mind.
Then the moon rose over the hermitage grounds, as if sprinkling them with rays white as the waves of the milk-ocean and laden with nectar.
Then the Blessed Jābāli, seated comfortably upon his own mat with his body bound in a cross-legged posture by his bark garment, began to speak.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, all of you listen with focused attention to this story,
which has been introduced by way of a preliminary account concerning that person."
In the land of Avanti, there exists a city named Ujjayinī, which is like the birthplace of the Fortune of Saṃsāra and a treasure-trove of all excellences.
Even those for whom Laṅkā, Alakā, and Amarāvatī are their beloved dwellings find no rest in them when they behold this [heavenly realm]. (AK 2.7)
What more need be said? For there Rudra himself, abandoning his delight in dwelling on Kailāsa, resides under the name Mahākāla.
In that city there was a glorious lord of the earth named Tārāpīḍa, who was like Bharata, Māndhātṛ, Bhagīratha, and Pṛthu, and who served as the ornament of the realm.
Where all the virtues, which were previously scattered here and there in mutual opposition, now dwell together with full confidence.
A pair:
By the power of their intellects, Bhṛgu’s descendant Śukra and Bṛhaspati were his ministers;
and there was also a brahmin minister named Śukanāsa. AK 2.11.
Having traversed this earth with his three strides,
that king deposited the burden upon that minister who was capable of bearing it.
And so that minister protected all his subjects in such a way that not even the slightest of the three kinds of suffering touched them.
And to the extent that the people in this world came to love him as a father,
to that same extent the king considered himself to have accomplished his purpose.
Therefore, he entrusted the acquisition of the world to his own arm without affliction;
yet, because it would have caused obstacles to his enjoyment, he placed its protection under the charge of the ministers.
Having accomplished his purpose and no longer thinking of any remaining tasks,
he sat at ease, having directed his delight toward the objects of the senses.
For the wealth and enjoyments of a king who has accomplished his purpose constitute his splendor;
yet for one whose desire to conquer remains unfulfilled, those very things are but a mockery.
That youth, possessing a charming appearance and a festival for the eyes of young women,
skilled in the arts and full of passion, enjoyed an abundance of pleasures.
There were no enjoyments for him, no games, no social gatherings, no flavors,
and no pleasures in which his mind did not reach the further shore.
Although that lord of the earth knew the grounds for enjoying every kind of pleasure,
he did not know even a single happiness arising from the sight of his offspring.
Just as his fresh youth passed away with the lapse of time,
so too did his grief increase because of his childlessness.
And among the entire assembly of women in the inner apartments,
the queen named Vilāsavatī was his chief consort, as dear to him as his own life.
Once, by her husband's permission, that queen went to an outer temple to worship Gaurī.
Then, while the Purāṇa was being recited, she heard there, as part of the context, a scriptural passage stating: "How can there be worlds for one who has no son? (AK 2.24)
Like a red-hot iron needle, that sacred teaching entered the interior of her ears, inflicting upon her an indescribable agony.
Then, having turned back and entered her own palace,
she sat upon the ground with her face veiled by her garment and wept.
Though entreated by her friends, she did not maintain her composure;
she did not rise to take food, nor did she cease from weeping.
Then, having learned of her suffering from her attendants, the king entered the inner apartments and spoke to her privately, seeking to appease her.
My dear, what is this that has begun? Why do you weep without cause?
Never before have you experienced anger on my account.
O beautiful one, who else would provoke your anger— who looks only to my face for guidance and whose very life depends on me— for whom you are angry?
When she said nothing at all despite being thus entreated,
the king was informed of what had transpired by her friend.
Then, on account of that occurrence, he too became overcome with grief and wept,
resting his tearful face upon the chest of his beloved.
Having wept for a long time, the king wiped his eyes himself and, falling silent,
spoke in a faltering voice while consoling the queen.
O Goddess, for me too, this anxiety has long been unbearable;
it torments my heart like an incurable disease.
Alas, my kingdom is fruitless; my wealth is fruitless;
my enjoyments are fruitless; my life is fruitless.
Whence could such a wealth of fortune come to us unfortunate ones,
that we might behold your lap adorned by you in your childhood?
When will my son, wishing for some toy, ever pull at the beard of me, a man of evil deeds, while speaking some indistinct words?
While he was thus lamenting with eyes clouded by tears,
Śukanāsa, having heard this news, arrived in haste.
He too has been rendered childless by the King of Fate as if he were slain;
and because of this grief for him, his wife weeps in the house.
But he, perceiving the suffering residing in his master as "suffering," and being intent on the means to remove that suffering, spoke wisely: AK 2.40.
Where is the nature of a steadfast deity, and where is this state of a distressed mind?
Grief finds no place in the hearts of those such as you.
If indeed the Queen has fallen into such dejection due to her female nature,
then why is it fitting for Your Majesty, with your long beard, to weep?
What is this sequence of action for attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, that one sighs for so long with the hand resting upon the cheek? (AK 2.43)
If, O Noble Lady, you truly find life difficult to bear because of childlessness, let your mind be fixed upon the Dharma; by doing so, you will attain the festival of Dharma.
Let wealth be given to the Brahmins; let all the deities be honored;
let water-stations and gardens be established; and let reservoirs be dug.
There is no human goal whatsoever in this world that cannot be attained by wise ones such as you who are devoted to the Dharma.
Having heard these and other words spoken by Śukanāsa, the couple rose up, their fever of anxiety dispelled, and performed all their daily duties as if they were in perfect health.
From that time forward, the two of them performed all kinds of diverse acts of charity, sacrifices, oblations, and austerities; consequently, all living beings were filled with wonder.
Then once, O protector of the earth, the king saw in a dream the unbroken moon entering the face of Vilāsavatī.
Likewise, Śukanāsa’s wife, named Manoramā,
was also seen by him in a dream, marked with a white lotus.
On the following day at sunrise, after performing the auspicious rites,
the king related that dream to Śukanāsa.
With joy, he said to him: "Your desires have been fulfilled;
before long, the queen shall give birth to a son as beautiful as the full moon."
Then, after some days had passed, the queen conceived; and the lord of men learned of this from her companions.
To them he gave variegated garments and ornaments;
as the signs of pregnancy became manifest in due course, he rejoiced all the more.
With eyes wide open in great joy, he spoke to Śukanāsa and longed for those days of her delivery, just as a *cātaka* bird longs for the clouds.
When the tenth month was complete, the queen gave birth to a son,
and through that joy, the entire world seemed to have turned over anew.

Seeing the vessel presented, filled with the joy of the great festival, the king could not contain it within himself, just as the three strides of Viṣṇu could not be contained within the three worlds.
Śukanāsa, however, embraced the king firmly around the neck;
out of eagerness, they both went to the lying-in chamber.
Then they beheld the youth, with every limb clearly manifest,
like the newly risen orb of the moon, moist with the glow of its emergence.

Śukanāsa, having carefully examined each limb of the infant, took hold of the king by the hand and spoke with words full of joy: AKad_2.60: "Having closely inspected each and every limb of the child, Śukanāsa took the king by the hand and spoke with a heart full of joy."
This is the conch, this the wheel, this the ūrṇā-hair, and this the lotus;
behold, the marks of a child who will become a universal monarch (cakravartin) are visible.
Do not entertain any doubt that he whom you saw in a dream as the moon entering the queen’s mouth is indeed this very person born here.
Thus, as those two were drenched by the nectar of the bliss arising from that sight,
the ocean of joy within Śukanāsa and the king increased all the more.
In the meantime, the doorkeeper, having come from the minister’s house,
announced the celebration for the birth of a son at Śukanāsa’s residence.
Then the lord of the earth repeatedly embraced Śukanāsa and himself removed his upper garment as a full vessel of honor.
And he said to him: "Behold this happiness of ours that surpasses all other happiness!
These rays of the moon have truly fallen here as frost."
Excellent is this which has been undertaken by the Creator, in accordance with our own minds,
since we have both been brought together as a single vessel for happiness and suffering.
Then, with the sounds of musical instruments, dances, and the rhythms of *carcarī* and *tāla*,
and with powders of vermilion, camphor, and the like, and with pastes of saffron;
In that great festival of the royal palace, a playful dalliance proceeded without restraint, indifferent to the conventional distinctions between high and low.
But the king, having observed such playful dalliance in his own home,
went to Śukanāsa’s house and caused that same pleasure to be performed there twofold.
Then, when the birth-rites and other ceremonies had been performed, and the vigil on the sixth night had taken place,
Vilāsavatī had bathed, and the pure time had arrived.
On an auspicious day, authorized by the astrologers,
the lord of the earth bathed and honored the best of the twice-born with a hundred thousand gold pieces.
Showering ornaments and garments upon the child’s attendants,
he bestowed upon him the dream-like name Candrāpīḍa.
Śukanāsa, having honored the brahmins in a manner befitting brahmins,
bestowed the name Vaiśampāyana upon his own son.
Then, growing up gradually and having had the auspicious tonsure ceremony and other rites performed,
Candrāpīḍa became the supreme ornament upon the laps of his parents.
With his moon-like form, with sweet and playful movements,
and with conversations in indistinct accents, he captivated the minds of the two of them.
Then, when the seventh year had arrived, the king had a school constructed for Candrāpīḍa outside the city, endowed with many excellent qualities.
And when he had been invested with the sacred thread at the time appropriate for a member of the kṣatriya caste,
the king established him there for the sake of attaining knowledge.
He appointed as teachers those who were experts in logic and grammar, proficient in the science of archery, and skilled in the art of government and other such disciplines.
Śukanāsa also, having brought his son forward according to the prescribed rites,
made him a follower of the prince while he resided in the house of learning.
The king went to see his son staying at the teacher's residence;
though entreated by the mother, he did not have him brought home.
Then the prince, having reached his sixteenth year and possessing an intellect as sharp as the tip of a kusha grass blade,
grasped the sciences upon being taught them once, as if they were already previously practiced.
He knew the true meaning of all treatises, was a master poet in all languages,
was a speaker in all philosophical systems, and was an expert in all branches of learning.
He was mature in all the arts, skillful in all tasks,
and his course was unerring in all worldly affairs.
Increasing gradually, he practiced physical exercise;
and through that practice, having attained perfection in all his limbs, he shone with splendor.
With long arms, broad shoulders, a wide chest, and a slender waist;
with deep-set arm-pits, rounded thighs, youthful, and possessing the gait of an elephant.
The son of Śukanāsa was like his reflection in all his qualities, except for the physical weight of his body and life-force.
But the king, having learned that his son had completed his purpose at the teacher’s house, proceeded to bring him home according to the words of Śukanāsa.
Having summoned his army commander named Balāhaka and performed auspicious rites on a holy day, he dispatched him to bring back his son.
And he dispatched a thousand princes, disciplined and strong of arm,
along with his son who followed him.
Likewise, he dispatched a horse named Indrāyudha,
which had surpassed Uccaiḥśravas by means of its various incomparable qualities.
Then Balāhaka went there and beheld the prince residing in the house of learning, and he bowed respectfully to him.
And he announced the king's command, "Please come to the palace," and introduced the princes to him by their names.
Then the princes, whose weightiness was due to virtues such as valor proclaimed by Balāhaka, bowed down to him as the immortals bow to Purandara.

Having caused the horse Indrāyudha—whose radiance produced a rainbow by the light of the jewels on its saddle—to enter, Balāhaka spoke again: AKBh 2.95: paryāṇaratnajyotirbhir janitendrāyudhaprabham / indrāyudhaṃ praveśyāśvaṃ punar āha balāhakaḥ // 2.95 //
Mount this jewel among horses, born of the Sindhu river and not from a womb,
which has been presented as a gift to Your Majesty by the King of Persia.
But Candrāpīḍa, seeing that unsurpassed horse, was struck with great wonder and reflected thus for a long time: AKad_2.97 //
"My heart tells me this: he is not truly a horse;
surely someone has attained the state of a horse through some curse."
This report concerning her not being born from a womb is witnessed by one's own resolve:
it is said that Rambhā, a daughter of the Apsarases, became a mare due to a curse.
This loftiness would belong either to Garuḍa or to Uccaiḥśravas;
it could arise from their splendor or their physical form, but not in ordinary horses.
Having thus reflected with his intellect, he then adorned himself with flower garlands, ornaments, and fine silken garments provided by Balāhaka.
Having taken leave of his gurus and received their blessings, and being praised by brahmins and bards,
he beheld Vaiśampāyana mounted upon another horse.
"Whoever you may be, homage to you! This transgression of ours in ascending [the mountain] must be forgiven by you," he said as he was climbing up. (AK 2.103)
Having ascended the Tilaka tree, which was adorned with a rainbow, he felt as if the entire three worlds had come into his possession, just as Acyuta did when mounting Vainateya.
Then, accompanied by Vaiśampāyana, he emerged from that palace and,
surrounded by the princes, entered the city slowly.
Then, standing at the windows of their palaces along the royal road, the young women beheld him as he passed by, possessed of incomparable beauty;
casting aside their heavy modesty, their limbs trembling with agitation, they honored him with eyes that betrayed the transformations born of love.
