it is so described in the scriptures. Therefore, rise quickly and let us go."
Having been addressed thus by her, I assumed an attire suitable for that occasion and,
placing her alone before me, departed from the house unobserved.
When you came to this place with steps as swift as eagerness,
my right eye throbbed again and again.
I heard, as it were, the sound of weeping in the forest;
because of that, suspicion having arisen, I went with even greater haste.
Having gone only a few steps, [he cried out]: "Alas, friend Puṇḍarīka, treasury of asceticism! Where have you gone, leaving the three worlds empty? (AK 4.106)
Alas! I am ruined, I am dissolved, I am consumed; what shall I do?
Having gone before my father Śvetaketu, what shall I say in his presence?
"O wicked Mahāśvetā, you are not satisfied even with this rosary;
for by you, the very life-force of my friend has been taken away."
"Friend, grant me this word: I cannot live without you.
Then I heard Kapiñjala lamenting in such words as these.
Then, with her limbs trembling and her steps faltering, she went to that place as if being carried there by someone, having uttered this prayer: *cakkalakam*.
Having gone there, I saw him at that very moment with his life departed;
he remained standing just so, as if angry, saying, "Why have you returned so late? (AK 4.111).
Having said this much, that maiden fell upon the surface of the rock as if wishing to speak further regarding her own story beyond this point, overcome by a swoon.
And beholding her with her consciousness lost, Candrāpīḍa considered himself a sinner who had acted improperly by questioning her.
Rising up in great agitation, he restored her consciousness with the breeze from plantain leaves and with cool,
clear waters.
Having regained consciousness and remembering her own calamity,
she wept and lamented as if experiencing it all over again.
At that time, even the hearts of the trees were broken by grief;
under the guise of their echoing sounds, even the quarters of the sky seemed to weep aloud.
Then Candrāpīḍa, his eyes choked with tears, said to her:
"Let it be; it is not possible to speak or to hear anything further than this."
Having somehow restrained the surge of her grief, she said:
"What else remains to be said or even heard beyond this?"
But, O Prince, that slight hope by which I sustain this wretched life only leads to affliction; I shall tell you of that wonder.
At that time, for that exceedingly intense burden of suffering, I perceived no remedy whatsoever other than death. (AK 4.120)
And having made firm my resolve for death, I prepared my arrangements;
then, from the orb of the moon, there emerged a certain man whose radiance was like snow.
Having descended from the sky to the surface of the earth and placed me within the cage of his arms,
he leapt back toward heaven and spoke to me with a noble voice, consoling me like a father.
"Cease from this effort toward death; O Mahāśvetā, my dear child, you shall be reunited with this beloved once again.
Hearing these words from him, filled with agitation and wonder, I asked Kapiñjala, who was standing there, "What is this? AKad_4.123.
"Having snatched away my dear friend, where are you going now?"—with these words, he cast an upward glance with a flash of fierce and violent rage;
yet, without giving heed to my speech, he bound his waist-cloth with extreme speed and likewise departed into the sky.
While I was watching, all three of them entered the orb of the cool-rayed moon; having abandoned their customary duties out of confidence in that [vision], I too took up this vow.

Then my father came here from there, and since that time he has remained here, for even with great effort he could not succeed in leading me back home; after staying for a very long time, he has now departed for his own house.

Thus ends the fourth canto in the *Kādambarī-kathāsāra*, a work composed by Abhinanda, the son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Jayanta, who was counted among the foremost of the most excellent and wise scholars.
Fifth Canto:
Having thus related in detail the full account of her own life story without artifice...
Mahāśvetā ceased speaking, her lower lip parched by her sighs.
Candrāpīḍa, however, reflecting upon that manifestation of the god of love,
spoke to her consolingly, though inwardly filled with trembling wonder.
Although it happened long ago, I—failing to perceive its transformation and with a mind possessed by curiosity—have brought my grief back to its freshness. (AK 5.3)
Therefore, O auspicious lady, you ought not to grieve in such a manner;
surely you have been comforted by the Lord Moon himself.
What other man, possessing such a form and such power, could be conceived as emerging from that mandala at night and entering back into it? (AK 5.5)
Various destinies of the deities are heard of in many ways,
produced by the diversity of boons, curses, asceticism, powers, and yogic attainments.
And Śvetaketu was his father, equal to Prajāpati;
for him, there was indeed nothing whatsoever that could not be accomplished through ascetic penances.
Having thus consoled Mahāśvetā with these and other arguments and illustrations from history, he questioned her again.
That friend of yours named Taralikā, who was so full of confidence and intimacy—where has she gone today, O Blessed One? For she never leaves you alone.
Then Mahāśvetā said: "Where is that poor woman going?
Listen, moreover, to the reason why she was sent by me."
That lord of the Gandharvas named Citraratha, whom I have described, was the one by whom this Lord Maheśvara was propitiated.
By him this lake named Acchoda was dug out with its exceedingly clear water,
and by him this grove named Caitraratha was created.
In that lineage of Apsarases born from the ocean of nectar,
there was a queen named Madirā, who was dearer to him than life itself.
Of those two, there is a daughter named Kādambarī, in the bloom of youth,
who seems to mock Lakṣmī herself with her beauty, charm, and grace.
From my very childhood, I have had such great love for her that people perceive the lives of us two as one and the same.
Having immediately learned this news concerning me,
that young woman undertook a vow, even though she was being restrained by her kinsmen.
"As long as Mahāśvetā does not reach the end of this sorrow,
so long must I not perform the taking of my own hand in marriage."
Therefore, in whatever measure her youthful beauty unfolds,
in that same measure Citraratha experiences the greatest distress because of it.
"Daughter, he has instructed me:
'Exert yourself with such diligence that your sister may loosen this knot of malignant possession.'"
Therefore, Taralikā was sent there by me, having been instructed extensively in accordance with the circumstances; she will return here again tomorrow.
Having thus passed the day in conversation at Mahāśvetā’s hermitage,
Candrāpīḍa performed the twilight rites when the sun had set.
There, having brought an *indrāyudha* (rainbow-colored reed) and bound it to a *nicula* tree somewhere in the region where Mahāśvetā had spoken, he prepared a bed of leaves.
As he sat there, though exhausted, he meditated for a long time upon that very same discourse, rich in wonders, exactly as he had heard it.
As he continued to think of the army, Vaiśampāyana,
and Pattralekhā, that night passed for him while he remained largely awake.
But even the horse Indrāyudha, with eyes moist with tears, cast upon the face of Mahāśvetā a gaze full of recognition, much like a human being.
When the night had passed and she had performed her morning rites,
Mahāśvetā, perceiving that [Kādambarī] had arisen from her meditation, went into her presence.
Then, after Candrāpīḍa had entered and the sun had risen not very far [above the horizon],
Taralikā departed from there along with the Gandharva prince.

Having entered, prostrated before Mahāśvetā, and sat down, she was asked by her, "Have you accomplished your purpose? and turning her neck, she replied: *sā praviśya mahāśvetāṃ praṇipatyopaviśya ca / siddhārthāsīti tatpṛṣṭā valitagrīvam abravīt //* AKad_5.28 *//*
O Princess, hear from the mouth of Keyūraka that message which was spoken by her upon hearing yours.
Then Keyūraka said: "Is it not the case that you do not recognize your own mind?
This mind of yours is none other than yourself; why then do you examine it as if it were another?"
Or rather, I am the proper object for this great reproach from you, who dwell in a penance grove while I remain in my own home.
Having heard your message from the mouth of Taralikā,
this reply has been delivered to you by your dear friend.
Having heard this, Mahāśvetā, with motionless eyes for a moment,
reflected on something within herself and then spoke to Candrāpīḍa.
O Prince, your appearance and your refined conduct are so exquisite that they inspire longing even in those who are free from desire, through their very totality.
You have heard these words of Kādambarī from Keyūraka;
what remedy is there for that, other than my going there myself?
Not far from here lies the capital city of the Gandharva king; behold it today through our guidance, for tomorrow you shall go to your own army.
By displaying this form of yours, so sublime and sweet,
I too would have rendered great service to the world of the Gandharvas.
But Candrāpīḍa said to her: "Enough of speaking at length;
the command of even the sages is not to be transgressed by me. (AK 5.38)
Then he set out to go with Mahāśvetā,
having directed Keyūraka toward the horse with a glance, while he himself proceeded on foot.
Keyūraka went before Kādambarī and announced his arrival,
as well as his appearance and his qualities that inspired wonder.
Having traveled some distance, Candrāpīḍa reached the city of the Gandharva king, which was like another Amarāvatī.
Having reached the capital city with its lofty crystal archways,
and having passed through seven courtyards, he entered the inner apartments of the princesses.
Then, having entered by the path pointed out by Keyūraka,
he beheld a magnificent pavilion with pillars made of radiant jewels.
In the midst of that [city], she sat upon a jeweled throne,
surrounded by a vast retinue of women adorned with variegated ornaments of precious gems.
By means of this radiance of her body, which outshines the luster of jewels,
she makes the quarters of the sky as bright as polished, molten gold.
Though he remained detached, he moistened others; though he did not break the rules of virtuous conduct, he was like a new ocean of beauty, surging with waves within.
With his eyes wide open, he beheld Kādambarī, who had attained the status of the standard of comparison for all things that could be compared.
Then, observing within her that perfection of beauty and loveliness which stood at the pinnacle of excellence beyond all others,
he reflected for a moment.
Truly, there is no limit to the Creator’s power in the fashioning of wonders,
he who was able to create such jewels as these.
The time of Hari, who bears Lakṣmī upon his chest, passes in vain;
and the Moon-crested Lord is cheated by bearing Gaurī with only half of his body.
What is the use of the thousand eyes of the wielder of the thunderbolt, which are unblinking,
if by them this [truth] is never seen, because his mind is not focused on anything else?
While he was reflecting in this way, the daughter of Citraratha then rose up in haste and went forward to meet Mahāśvetā.
But Mahāśvetā, having embraced her without hesitation and with an abundance of affection,
spoke to her while first mentioning Candrāpīḍa.
For this is Candrāpīḍa, the son of the universal monarch Tārāpīḍa, who has come here to the land of Bhārata.
Let there be a great festival for the entire family of the Gandharvas by this one who has entered here and dwells within the range of their vision.
Then Kādambarī cast her gaze upon him for a long time— a gaze that opened wide with the raising of her eyelashes and extended to the corners of her eyes as far as her ears.
Then, through that very door opened by his own power of illusion,
Madana entered within and took hold of her heart.
When Candrāpīḍa was seated upon a jeweled throne,
the two daughters of Haṃsa and Citraratha sat near him and engaged in a conversation.
Then Mahāśvetā forcibly established the household duties upon Candrāpīḍa, while Kādambarī sat there, motionless with shame.
Her dear friend named Madalekhā, who was no different from Kādambarī’s own body,
performed the washing of her feet.
But Kādambarī, her sprout-like hands perspiring and trembling,
offered herself to him under the pretext of betel.
Her mind captivated by the sweetness of the touch of his finger-tips,
she did not notice that the jeweled bracelet had slipped from her hand.
Candrāpīḍa, too, by the excellence of the bliss arising from the touch of her hand,
then considered himself like the sovereign of the three worlds.
Then, while the entire company of maidens sat in silence,
a quarrel broke out between a parrot and a maina for the sake of sport.
And in that context, to increase their quarrel with a sarcastic remark,
Candrāpīḍa said something by which all the women burst into laughter.
And those words of Candrāpīḍa— sweet-toned and washing the quarters of the sky with the luster of his teeth— captivated Kādambarī’s mind all the more.
Then, after a mere moment had passed, the chamberlain entered and said:
"The Queen wishes to see you two princesses without any hindrance."
Having placed Candrāpīḍa, who was seated comfortably in a daughter’s delightful pleasure-mansion on the Play-Mountain, [the messenger] approached his mother’s presence.
There, the principal female companions of Kādambarī, led by Keyūraka, attended upon Candrāpīḍa as he sat upon the couch.
He performed the acts of bathing, anointing, and eating with the provisions brought by him,
which were provided through riches that could have been attained even in the city of the immortals.
Then, as the sun’s radiance grew dim, Kādambarī,
accompanied solely by Madalekhā, ascended to the top of her great palace.
And standing there, she gazed upon Candrāpīḍa, who was situated on the pleasure-mountain,
with a glance whose outer corners reached as far as her ears.
At that moment, Candrāpīḍa’s side-long glances with their sharp tips fell upon her at the same time as the arrows of the flower-armed god.
And as if drinking in that loveliness which was quickly brought near by their side-long glances that had already effected a union, she spoke to Madalekhā:
"O friend, I have never even heard the name 'Madana' mentioned in stories;
today, that very form of Candrāpīḍa has been seen by me directly."
Nothing was said by Mahāśvetā regarding the matter at hand;
nevertheless, as she brought him here, everything was communicated without words.
Could it be that she perceived my transformation at that time?
Or how could she not have perceived it, since she herself had witnessed the agitation caused by love?
Even now, I shall withdraw this transformation of the mind, however gross it may be, which is contrary to my own resolve.
However, this necklace of Śeṣa is an ornament suited to his form;
let it be quickly fastened by you upon his chest, even against his will.
Madalekhā, having taken that necklace and gone into his presence,
spoke to him in such a way that he replied to her with nothing at all.
Then Madalekhā placed a necklace upon his neck,
its radiance as noble as the rays of the autumnal moon filling the quarters of the sky.
And Candrāpīḍa, adorned with the necklace,
shone like the full moon surrounded by a multitude of stars.
And Kādambarī, having gazed upon him for a long time, slowly descended from that palace roof at the arrival of night.
Then, having risen and performed the rites of twilight, Candrāpīḍa supported his body upon the bed, but his mind rested upon anxiety.
Are these the innate graces of a Gandharva maiden,
or is it that the God of Love is making this young girl dance for the sake of this person?
Just as her glance behaves like a clever messenger,
so does this suspicion dwell within my mind.
I recognize that the sequence of following the Kinnaras has indeed flowered;
however, through the transformation of time, I do not know what it will bear as fruit.
Or perhaps this delusion of mine is caused by the intoxication of youth;
what connection could there be between a human and a Gandharva? What is the point of that?
Let this self-conceit of mine, which follows such an improper course, be set aside; for everything is revealed by time—how then could my soldiers [not be overcome]?
As he was thinking thus, sleep, accumulated over a long time,
caused his eyes to become like closed buds until the end of the night.
Then, having risen on the following day and performed his morning rites,
he saw Kādambarī and Mahāśvetā as if he had found them after a long time.
Having received his permission and surrounded by the Gandharvas he had commanded,
he mounted the Indrāyudha chariot and set out toward the army.
Then, by some means,
he beheld his own army encamped on the shore of the lake, having regained its way.
Having seen all those kings there, he made Pattralekhā— the son of the minister who knew his own history— his confidant in private, especially so.
When that night had passed and the sun had risen on the following day,
Keyūraka came from Hemakūṭa and spoke to him.
"Kādambarī, not being clever, desires to see you constantly; she has forgotten to bring the remaining necklace to your bed. (AKad 5.96)
Having heard this from Keyūraka and having met with Pattralekhā,
Candrāpīḍa then quickly returned once more to Hemakūṭa.
Having paid homage to Mahāśvetā, whose arrival she had praised,
he then beheld Kādambarī, preceded by Pattralekhā.
In a snow palace fashioned on the bank of a lotus pond in a garden,
she sat upon a bed of plantain leaves, her body withered.
At the mere sight of him, she felt as if repeatedly comforted;
though wishing to rise from there, she remained lying down at his word.
Then, purified by the mere pleasure of inquiring after each other's welfare,
their conversations proceeded, moistened with various playful jests.
Having stayed there for a long time in that manner, he clearly made known his own intention to her, who was under his control, through various indirect expressions.
At her request, having dispatched Pattralekhā to her presence,
he returned once more to the camp accompanied by Keyūraka.
Then, having observed that a messenger had arrived from Ujjayinī the previous day, he read the letter himself.
Then, having understood his father’s command which foretold his swift return,
he placed that letter in Keyūraka’s hand with his eyes narrowed.
Then, having consulted with the son of his minister for that purpose, and reflecting, "So be it," he resolved upon his departure.
"I speak the truth: my heart, which relishes your favor, does not wish to go to that place; however, this command of my guru must not be transgressed.
Let your anger be endured for now; I shall return here once more after having delivered a message to Kādambarī. Thus he sent Keyūraka away with words choked by tears.
He addressed Vaiśampāyana: "You shall follow behind, tending the army; I shall go quickly from here with a few horses.
Having thus resolved, he set out as soon as the drum for the march was struck, and having traveled some distance, he took up residence on the bank of a Caṇḍikā hermitage that day.

There, passing the night in diversions consisting of stories regarding the conduct, dress, speech, ascetic practices, and spiritual attainments of arrogant Dravidian religious men, he reached Ujjayinī quickly in a few days by means of constant, unimpeded journeys.
Thus ends the fifth canto in the *Kādambarī-kathāsāra*, the work of Abhinanda, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Jayanta, who was counted among the foremost of the most excellent scholars.
The Sixth Canto:
Then, having entered the city and attended upon his parents for a long time, he—
And he entered again the prince's residence, where Śukanāsa resided.
There, for him whose one-pointed mind was absorbed in meditation on Kādambarī,
there was nothing— whether stationary or moving— that could bring him pleasure.
He did not take pleasant food, nor did he perceive sweet flavors;
he took no delight in garments, nor did he apply ointments.
Like a traveler lost from his caravan, like an elephant strayed from its herd,
or like a young fawn caught in the snare of a net.
Meditating on the night by day and longing for the arrival of day at night,
he gazed incessantly toward the northern direction alone with tearful eyes.
Knowing that I have come from Keyūraka and the others, how will she treat me?
What will she say to Pattralekhā, or what will she herself be told by her?
Thus meditating day and night, without having attained any peace,
Candrāpīḍa passed some time in this manner.
Such was the outward appearance of this man of hidden nature that his parents did not perceive his true emptiness.
Then, as the days passed, Pattralekhā arrived in his presence,
having perfected her skill on the path through her training with Balāhaka’s troop of horses.
Candrāpīḍa, too, upon seeing her, felt his heart swell with joy;
he regarded her as Kādambarī herself and touched her again and again.
Then, feeling confident, he asked: "Tell me the story of Kādambarī;
does she remember us? What is the purpose of her coming here while we are angry?"
Looking at Candrāpīḍa as if with envy, she said: "O Prince, what is this anxiety? Devote yourself steadfastly to serving your elders."
For she was bestowed upon you by the God of Love himself,
who was deeply enamored, just as Fortune was bestowed upon the Lord of Wealth by the Ocean through the power of destiny.
Why have you pointlessly cast that young girl— who is as tender with fresh emotion as a young tree— into the fierce forest fire of separation?
Having learned of your arrival from the mouth of Keyūraka, O King,
she trembled like a stalk of rice struck by a thunderbolt.
O Pattralekhā, as long as he has not yet attained stability, how can such a thing be right for him—
that I believe even the *rākṣasas* would not do?
From that time forth, as her sighs grew like the passing days,
she gradually wasted away, like a summer night.
Having previously approached her due to habit, yet not having obtained the fragrance of her flowers,
the bees now avoid her braid from afar.
Her eyes, their kohl long forgotten, had their outer corners reddened by weeping; having abandoned their natural sweetness, they had turned to a state of bitterness.
For a long time she has abandoned her decorative paintings of leafy creepers; now she applies a fresh ornament to her cheeks: a necklace of pearls formed by teardrops.
Her lower lip, soft and naturally red, is brought to a state of withering by her sighs and her [faltering] voices, which are intensified by the increasing heat [of her passion].
And during her separation, her breasts were not at all covered by the pearl necklaces,
camphor, and sandalwood applied as remedies for the burning heat of her grief.
"The fire of her separation is not extinguished by the streams of the essence of her beauty, nor does the submarine fire find peace through the ocean; this is a pair of wonders. (AK 6.23)
Now like a female swan in a lake, now like a doe in a grove,
and now like a female ruddy goose on a sandbank, she wallows in distress again and again.
Having embraced you for a moment as you were conjured by her imagination before her, she now sees you in the void; embarrassed, she falls to the ground with her vine-like arms outstretched.
"Lest this one, having been censured, should go far even from mere thought"—
thinking thus, she does not censure you even with her mind, as if out of fear.
Her meditation now consists of your form; her speech is inclined toward your lineage; and her gaze is fixed upon your body. (AK 6.27)
How much can be described of her suffering from separation from the Supreme?
For that is accessible only through self-awareness and is experienced by her alone.
With her lower lip quivering repeatedly as if desiring to say something, she is restrained by some heavy weight residing within her heart.
Once, with her limbs writhing upon the ground like a female serpent,
she looked toward the quarters and, placing her face upon my lap, spoke.
"Arise and go; bring her back if you wish me to live, for I am unable to travel this very great distance."
As long as you remain, I live by your touch in whatever way it may be;
but once you have gone for even a short time, my vital breaths cannot endure.
"Having heard this and having seen it, I have come here;
beyond this, Your Majesty is the authority," she said, and weeping, she fell silent.
Having heard that, Candrāpīḍa became as if he had lost his memory;
then, having regained his memory, he reflected for a long time on the reason for his own departure.
Then, as the days passed, Keyūraka also arrived quickly to report the condition of Kādambarī, his mount exhausted by the long journey.
Entering the splendor of Ujjayinī, he was struck with wonder and thought,
"It is no wonder that my mind has become attached to this mistress."
Having entered, Candrāpīḍa was seen by him, emaciated in form,
solitary like a cakravāka bird, overwhelmed by separation from his beloved.
Seated upon his couch with his body languid, he was being fanned by Pattralekhā, who stood at his side holding a fly-whisk.
Having prostrated and sat down, he was touched deeply on the head by Candrāpīḍa, who respectfully inquired after his welfare.

Then, questioned by him regarding the news of Kādambarī, Keyūraka looked at Pattralekhā’s face and spoke these words in brief: AKad_6.40: "Then, questioned by him regarding the news of Kādambarī, Keyūraka looked at Pattralekhā’s face and spoke these words in brief."
"You have been addressed by her with nothing at all; if you were not addressed, why do you remain here?
Since you have been addressed and yet remain here, my purpose for coming has already been accomplished."
Nevertheless, being thus urged by him, "Speak your message," Keyūraka spoke again: "Indeed, you shall not be informed of anything false."
"How can separation from you, while you are still alive, destroy me?"—
it was by her meaningful glance that I was sent away, not by her words.
What is the use of saying much more here? Her agony of separation is such that even now my mind wavers as to whether she still lives.
Then, having remained for a long time on that day engaged in such conversations,
Candrāpīḍa had Keyūraka prepare a comfortable dwelling.
"If I were not a Rākṣasa, nor a Caṇḍāla, nor a Kirāta,
you would know me in every way as one who has reached the shore of Lake Acchoda."
Having instructed Keyūraka with these words, "On another day," she sent him away together with Pattralekhā, adorned with jewels.
When those two had departed, he remained with a deeply distressed mind,
contemplating some sign that would incline his thoughts toward going [forth].
Then he heard from those appointed [to inform him] that the army camp had arrived and,
moreover, had established its encampment at a distance of two yojanas.
Thinking, "I shall obtain some reason [to leave] from Vaiśampāyana," he went out from his father's camp to meet him by his father's command.
There, having observed the royal party announced by Balāhaka,
he asked the commander-in-chief, "Where indeed is Vaiśampāyana’s dwelling?"
But Balāhaka, his gaze cast downward, repeatedly scratching the earth, spoke with a choked voice: "Vaiśampāyana is certainly not here."
Then, having dismounted from his horse and sat down beneath a tree, he began to weep, lamenting, "Alas, my friend! *AKad_6.53*
Then Balāhaka, having fallen at the feet of Candrāpīḍa, said: "O Lord, do not act thus; he is indeed alive. AKad_6.54.
But Candrāpīḍa said to him: "I cannot believe it;
Vaiśampāyana does not leave me for even a moment while he is still alive."
To him, whose mind was thus bewildered, Balāhaka spoke again:
"Listen, O King, to how he came here and what occurred."
O King, having followed you as you set out after giving such a command,
he then turned back and remained right there in his usual state.
Then, having risen on the following day and performed his customary duties,
he wandered through the forest regions to divert his mind.
There, examining each place with recognition,
he, with eyes wide with alarm, desired to search for something as if it were lost.
Then, as the sun was facing the setting [mountain], we said to him:
"Stay today; you shall see the forest regions tomorrow."
Then, even as he was wandering about, he spoke as if with indignation: "Go!
You must not go; I shall not leave this place for as long as I live."
He remained right there for many days, wandering in the forest;
and by no means whatsoever was he able to be moved from that place.
Though he was not entreated by this entire circle of kings— who had performed the fast unto death and fell daily at his feet— he did not abandon his resolve.
Then, having stayed there for a long time and seeing no further business to be done, he said:
"The army has arrived here; you are the authority from this point forward."
Having heard this, Candrāpīḍa fell into a state of distress caused by grief and wonder; he remained just as he was, having taken his seat at the foot of the tree.
Then, having learned this news, the king, together with his ministers and the women of the inner apartments,
went to that very place without waiting for further details.
Having stood there for a moment as it were, and having personally questioned Balāhaka,
the lord of the earth spoke to Candrāpīḍa as if reproaching him.
Surely, O ill-mannered one, you have provoked his anger,
by which, throbbing within him, he has today abandoned you and taken refuge in the forest.
Never before have you two been seen separated for even a moment;
what has happened now that you are here in your home while he is in the forest of asceticism?
Indeed, without a specific cause, it is impossible to endure the heavy suffering of separation from mother, father, friends, kinsmen, country, or wealth. (AK 6.70)
When the king had spoken thus, Śukanāsa thereafter addressed him with his agitation suppressed, although grief was throbbing within him.

Why do you speak thus, even though you are one whose intellect is trained, without having investigated the reality of things and without reflecting upon them, relying merely on a conjectural inference? AK 6.72.
A rain of firebrands from the moon, or the growth of thorns from milk,
or the wrath of a child— whose source of credibility could such things possibly be?
That very same wicked and ill-born parrot, though taught for a very long time,
is one in whom even the essence of nectar, when sown, has borne fruit like the *kālakūṭa* poison.
Therefore, O Prince, you who are the sole life-force for the entire earth,
you ought not to bear the burden of grief on account of that evil-minded man.
When he had finished speaking, Candrāpīḍa fell at his father’s feet and, with palms joined in reverence and a throat choked with tears, spoke.
"Father, this is my penance for having suspected a fault;
you ought to grant me permission to go and bring him here."
Having observed him when he has arrived here and having questioned him under oath,
you will then come to know my merits or faults in due order.
Without bringing him back from where he stays, I shall not enter this house again; let this be my firm resolve.
When he had spoken thus, the king, his eyes clouded with tears,
did not look at the face of the minister, yet he spoke much there.
Although Candrāpīḍa was detained by his father and that minister through the employment of every possible means, he did not waver from his resolve.
Drenching his head with streams of tears, the beautiful woman,
lamenting piteously, awakened him after a long time.
While you remain, I behold my little son seated upon my own lap;
surely I shall become blind once you, my son, have departed.
Although he was thus long made tender by Vilāsavatī with her compassionate words, he did not abandon his resolve.
Then, with a voice whose syllables were choked and faltering, obstructed by a flood of tears, the king somehow spoke: "O son, as you know."
Then, having received permission from his father, he bowed to all his gurus and listened to their blessings,
while the flow of his tears was restrained with effort.
Having dismissed the kings who were weary on the road as best he could, Candrāpīḍa set forth with a very small retinue.
With a mind tormented by grief, wondering "What have I said?",
the king also slowly entered the city together with his army.
But the general Balāhaka, despite being restrained by the king,
did not enter his own home and followed after Candrāpīḍa.
Then, as Candrāpīḍa proceeded, eager for the sight of his beloved,
he regarded the region between Kailāsa and Vindhya as if it were mere straw.
As he rushed along with his rainbow-bow, he took no account of the trees, the mountains, the rivers, or the forest glades; nor did he distinguish between night and day.
Then the rainy season began, with its full and swelling clouds,
appearing like a beloved woman moist with the nine sentiments, come forth to welcome him.
Disregarding even that, he continued on his way and after a few days reached the shore of Lake Acchoda, whose waters were untroubled.
Having removed his ornaments and changed his two garments,
he then went to that hermitage to see Mahāśvetā.
There he saw Mahāśvetā, abashed by the sight of him,
speaking of her own wickedness with piteous, lamenting tones.
Having gazed with an eye whose lashes were the outflow of delusion consisting in ignorance of its cause, Candrāpīḍa questioned her, and she replied.
Having learned from Keyūraka that you had arrived by your father’s command,
you stayed for several days in Kādambarī’s residence.
Then, having arrived and seated myself here in this grove of asceticism according to custom,
I beheld a young brahmin wandering through the forest thickets.
Having recognized me with a look of mutual recognition, he, drawn toward me by love,
greatly agitated me with his playful jests and witty banter.
Then, even though he was being rebuked and strenuously restrained,
he remained for many days in that manner, tormenting me.
Once, however, while I was lying down at night, a shameless man, afflicted by the god of love, approached me with palms joined in supplication and begged for the reward of sexual union.
Then, having uttered "Fie! in anger and drawing water from his water-pot, I invoked the deities with meditation and cursed him.
By the color of your face, you have been taught only how to speak like a parrot;
go far away, O man of evil conduct, for you shall become nothing more than a parrot.
Whether by that great curse, or by the fire of passion, or by the evil karma accumulated in previous births,
or by the wondrous conduct of the Blessed One, he released his life-breaths and fell to the earth.
The next day, while my attendants were wailing in their own grief, I learned that he was your friend, the son of Śukanāsa.
Therefore, look upon me—shameless, pitiless, treacherous, and unworthy—who am the cause of the separation from my dear companion. (AK 6.105)
Having heard this, as if suddenly pierced by the tip of a spear, Candrāpīḍa cried out, "O lotus-faced Kādambarī, when shall I see you again?
Even as he spoke thus, his heart bursting with grief, he gave up his life at that very moment and fell to the surface of the earth like a tree.

Then, beholding him fallen upon the earth with his limbs relaxed, his neck bent, his white-cornered eyes closed, casting a slender and piteous light slowly toward the quarters of the sky, the helpless Mahāśvetā could not, for some time, dissolve even bit by bit.

Then the sun of fierce radiance, his power diminished, went to its setting; unable to behold the earth as if it were wretched, he left the world empty by making the cakravāka birds cry out piteously like elephants; and with his upward-reaching rays, he emitted a sound like a cry for protection against the unrighteous.
Thus ends the sixth canto in the *Kādambarī-kathāsāra*, the work of Abhinanda, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Jayantasūnu, who was counted among the foremost of the most excellent and wise teachers.
The Seventh Canto: At that moment, the Creator— who brings about the wondrous variety of manifold illusions— brought the young Kādambarī to that very place.
For she had undoubtedly learned from the mouths of Pattralekhā and Keyūraka that Candrāpīḍa had arrived.
Then she desired to go out to meet him as he arrived at Mahāśvetā’s hermitage— a place free from constraint and worthy of the full confidence of all.
Immediately following the account of Vaiśampāyana’s disappearance,
Candrāpīḍa suffered mental anguish born of separation from his friend.
Suspecting that Kādambarī was the cause for Mahāśvetā’s consolation, she recognized her and hurried toward her arrival.
Having instructed her, "Let Taralikā come quickly to my house," she sent her off; and she, having gone swiftly, spoke thus.
Then Kādambarī, her heart brimming with enthusiasm at Mahāśvetā’s message, conceived in her mind a profound longing to depart.
She was accompanied by her friend Madalekhā, who was as dear to her as her own heart and skilled in the preparation of betel, perfumes, and other such luxuries.
Placing Patralekhā, who was skilled in conversing about her beloved, at the forefront,
he went to that very place on that same day along with Keyūraka.
And as she was approaching, a succession of ill omens appeared for that young girl, causing her heart to tremble.
When the sun had set and the lord of night had risen, the vicinity of Mahāśvetā’s hermitage became a lake of deeply heated compassion.
And having reached that place, he then heard the sound of piteous weeping,
echoed by the mountain caves at the edge of the forest.
"I suspect that she herself has arrived here along this path," thinking thus as if filled with apprehension, he quickly entered the hermitage.
Then, having entered, she beheld her lord of life situated in that manner,
and Mahāśvetā, weeping bitterly with cries of distress.
Beholding Mahāśvetā overwhelmed by burgeoning grief,
she wept and fell into a swoon, her chest struck with intense pain.
Patralekhā too, gazing upon that moon-like Cāndrāpīḍa,
suddenly lost her composure and fell like a stone.
Questioned with fortitude by Kādambarī, Taralikā then related everything that had occurred regarding the sequence of her death.
Having heard that, Mahāśvetā cast off the despondency appropriate for women; regaining her composure, she spoke to Madalekhā.
I am now exhausted by this heavy weeping, which has been flowing in a continuous, thick stream for a long time.
I go according to what is appropriate; indeed, I am unable to weep.
My friend, the path has been shown to me by my great-souled Lord himself.
Due to the separation from his friend, he neither wept nor lamented; rather, he cast off his very life-breaths, saying, "Where has that path of mine gone? (AK 7.21)
"It is fitting, friend Mahāśvetā, that you should live in such a manner;
for you have been restored to life by the deities with the hope of being reunited with him."
But I, whose desires have been shattered in every way by fate,
what shall I do with these unfortunate life-breaths, excluded from all that is auspicious?
"Madalekhā, you must act in such a way that my father and mother, remaining steadfast in their family duties,
do not abandon their fortitude through the torment of separation from me."
You yourself must reside in my dwelling,
so that the conch shells may rest within the jeweled windows.
The prince, depicted there in a painting by my own hand,
must be protected so that he does not perish, even though he remains fixed within the picture.
Somewhere at the head of the bed, a painting of Kāmadeva, which has been worshipped in vain, should be placed against the jeweled wall.
A pleasure-mountain should be given to a tranquil ascetic;
for it was inhabited by the Prince, and it does not shine upon anyone else.
In the midst of my long pond garden, adorned with clusters of lotuses,
there dwells a flock of royal swans who have made their home there.
Nearby is a pleasure-pool filled with water from fountains,
and a fresh pleasure-grove which I myself have sprinkled with affection.
On that Bakula tree, Mālatī has just performed her wedding;
I have removed her marriage bracelet, but you yourself must remove it.
And this young *aśoka* tree has been adopted by me as a son;
it must be nurtured with water poured from my own hands, resembling the flow of breast milk.
Not seeing me repeatedly in the house, that fawn-eyed one will surely remain like a doe; you must lead her to the forest.
Act at every moment in such a way that this parrot of mine, who is prone to jesting, and that sārikā, Kālinī, do not engage in quarreling.
This female mongoose, who has always been cherished in my lap,
must be made to sleep on my own breast so that she does not go far away.
What is to be done with this long anxiety at home?
Quickly prepare the funeral pyre and kindle the blazing fire.
"Keyūraka, why do you look upon me so long and so piteously?
Arise, gather wood, and prepare the sacrificial fire!"
How can this body, composed of the water of loveliness, be reduced to fire?
It would be better for me to take this youth and fall into the water.
While the prince’s life was being abandoned at that very moment due to the grief for his friend, I have lived for all this time; for that, I am ashamed of myself.
"‘When shall I see you?’—having said this to me, he departed; now, seeing that she is delaying, he would say the very same thing. (AK 7.40)
Thus, upon seeing Kādambarī, who had just resolved upon death,
the moon became as if trembling.
By that [sound], the entire assembly of maidens became as if bathed by the surging waves of the Ocean of Milk, and they began to play the lute of their teeth.
Then a certain person of divine appearance, stationed in the sky, spoke with a voice as deep and steady as the thundering of a mass of clouds: AKad_7.43.
For you, my child Mahāśvetā, were previously comforted by me:
"Your beloved Puṇḍarīka still remains by my side even today. (AKad 7.44)
But let this Candrāpīḍa, the beloved of Kādambarī, remain right here for a short while, appearing as if asleep, his radiance unwavering.
For by this [life], having once again obtained a stable lifespan free from misfortune,
he shall bring to Kādambarī the joy of a firm embrace around the neck.
"May this firm conviction in your minds remain exactly as it is; let no transformation born of the nature of the elements touch it. (AK 7.47)
Having spoken thus, he suddenly vanished by means of that light;
at that moment, all the young women were filled with wonder.
And Pattralekhā, having regained her senses by that very word of Jyotirasa, rose up and went with rapid steps.
Taking that horse named Indrāyudha by its mane,
he entered the depths of the water together with it.
And as if apprehensive, Taralikā followed her who was moving with haste;
she saw Kapiñjala rising up from the midst of the water.
Having approached, he related what he had seen in its wondrous nature;
by that, the astonishment of those maidens increased all the more.
Then Kapiñjala was seen wearing slender matted locks bristling with drops of trickling water, his bark garment wet from the water.
Approaching Mahāśvetā herself, he said:
"O Princess, is this person even recognized by you?"
I am Kapiñjala, the friend of that one who is dear to you;
I am not to be reproached by you for his long absence.
"You have heard these words of the moon from Kādambarī;
now you two should hear my own account as well."
When my friend had been thus lifted up and carried away by him at that very moment,
I leaped into the sky and followed after him.
Then, having leaped far up and entered the lunar orb, he looked back at me who had already entered and said this: AK 7.58.
"O Kapiñjala, know me to be Mṛgāṅka;
I am he who was cursed in vain by that friend of yours while you were at Hemakūṭa."
For the course of worldly affairs must be sustained by me through my role as a guardian of the world;
thus, having arisen at my proper time, I shall spread forth my rays.
His passion greatly increased by the touch of my rays,
his life-breath almost reaching his throat, he looked at me with a harsh glare and uttered a curse.
"Just as I have been struck down by you today while afflicted by separation,
so too, O Moon, shall you die in birth after birth."
"I too have cursed him: 'You shall die just like me,' my anger provoked by the pain of his curse upon one who was innocent."
Then, as I perceived that he was my son-in-law through his connection with Mahāśvetā, a feverish distress, as it were, arose within me, though my anger had become very slight.
Even Śvetaketu, of great ascetic power, might provide a remedy;
I shall protect his body with my nectar-like rays.
Having thus lifted him up, I have brought him here; you, however, must go quickly and report this account to Śvetaketu.
Having heard these words of the Moon, as I was flying up toward heaven,
I hurriedly overtook a certain celestial being traveling in a chariot.
And out of anger, he cursed me by the power of his asceticism as if with a horse:
"Since I have been overstepped by you, you shall therefore become a horse."
Having prostrated before him, I said to that friend whose mind was blinded by grief:
"Out of negligence—and not out of pride in my asceticism—withdraw your anger toward me."
But he replied: "This curse has been pronounced; it cannot be otherwise.
It concerns the son of Tārāpīḍa, who is performing austerities in Ujjayinī."
The moon will visibly become the son of the king;
Puṇḍarīka [will be the son] of his minister, Śukanāsa.
"You shall become the mount for Indu, the son of Tārāpīḍa;
at the end of his life, upon bathing, your curse will come to an end."
Having heard that, I immediately fell into the ocean, overcome by the curse;
then, having become a horse, I rose up, not born from a womb.
"Even though I have become a horse, my memory has never failed me;
this very person was brought here by me through the sequence of following the Kinnaras."
This curse, involving a reciprocal exchange between the two of them,
was such that it must certainly come to pass for them through the connection of a second birth.
Therefore, I shall go to relate what has occurred to Śvetaketu,
and to find out where their second birth took place.
Having recognized that Puṇḍarīka was indeed Vaiśampāyana in disguise through the story of Kapiñjala, Mahāśvetā was consumed by remorse.
"In this second birth as well, I alone was born to bring about his death;
he was cursed by me because he was devoted to me," she lamented.
Then Kapiñjala restrained her as she was weeping in this way, and said: "The limit has been reached; for the most part, the period of suffering is now at its end."
For in a very short time, you shall again place the rosary with a smile upon the sprout-like hand of Puṇḍarīka.
Kādambarī, too, shall be delighted by the dense words of Candrāpīḍa, which are enriched by the nectar of his sweet and charming smiles.
Kādambarī asked him, "Venerable sir, where is she who is called Pattralekhā? He replied, "I have not learned her whereabouts."
Having spoken thus, Kapiñjala then flew up into the sky, scattering drops of water from his pores that were indistinguishable from droplets of the Acchoda lake.
When he had departed, Mahāśvetā and Kādambarī likewise spent that night with her,
conversing amidst grief, wonder, and trembling.
Through the narrative of Mahāśvetā’s life, she gained even greater certainty and produced a firm conviction in Kādambarī’s heart.
Then, on the following day, he placed her upon a charming terrace made of expansive crystal slabs,
which was bristling with particles of camphor and frost.
Having sprinkled him with clear waters and anointed his body with sandalwood paste,
Kādambarī worshipped Candrāpīḍa’s form for a long time.
"If this assurance is true, then all is well;
otherwise, where will my death go? she resolved within herself.
And she said to Mahāśvetā: "Indeed, I am not ashamed now to address you as 'friend,' for you are a fellow-student in suffering."
By acting according to the prescribed rule and sharing in our joys and sorrows alike,
you have not defiled the long-established friendship between us two.
From that time forward, the female ascetic remained worshipping the image of Candrāpīḍa day and night, as if it were the moon-crested Śiva himself.
Then, as the days passed, observing that Candrāpīḍa’s body remained free from change, she formed a firm hope.
Then, having summoned the commander-in-chief Balāhaka, he addressed him:
"The entire matter and the highly wondrous account are known to you."
Since we have gained confidence by the fact that the radiance of your body has not perished,
you ought to go to Ujjayinī for the sake of comforting our lord.
He replied: "O Queen, I shall send another well-known person there;
having left the crown prince behind here, I do not venture to go myself."
Then a close attendant of the king named Tvaritaka was dispatched,
along with a letter bearing characters written by his own hand.
Having gone and reached Ujjayinī, he reported everything to the king;
the king, along with his harem and ministers, heard it all in due order.
Then, his mind bewildered by hearing of the shattering of his son's heart,
he lacked firm conviction regarding the subsequent account.
But Śukanāsa said to him: "O King, what delusion can there be for you here, who know the variety of karma and have heard the Itihāsas and the Śāstras?"
Indeed, it is heard in the Purāṇas and also recited in the Smṛtis that gods and sages assume human bodies.
The diverse and extraordinary excellences of men, which are appropriate for superhuman beings,
are capable of inferring some kind of non-worldly seed.
And the prince does not differ greatly from the moon in his virtues;
where else among other men has such radiance, such form, and such power ever been seen?
In a dream, you saw the moon entering the mouth of a goddess;
and I beheld a Brahmin woman marked with a white lotus.
For them, it was indeed a curse; but for us two, it was a supreme boon—that deities should attain the state of being sons in the homes of those subject to mortal nature.
Furthermore, how could Kapiñjala, whose movement in the sky was likewise unimpeded, speak falsely? And where indeed is there a horse such as that?
Where else has this been seen? That the body, composed of the five elements, does not undergo transformation even when one has abandoned life.
"Tvaritaka might speak falsely, and Balāhaka might write falsely;
such a suspicion is not appropriate for you, who have well-examined your servants. (AK 7.107)
You shall soon behold the world filled with an incomparable and radiant joy,
like the prince Kumāra when he was released from the Rāhu-like eclipse of the curse and its torment, like the moon freed from the demon of the eclipse.
Although the king heard these words of his ministers, his mind— distraught by affection for his own son—
could find no steadiness and instead resolved upon departure.

Then, accompanied by his queens whose eyes were filled with tears and joined by his own ministers, the king went to the bank of the Acchoda lake; and as he departed, all the people of the countryside and the city followed after him, their every hope relaxed.
When he had departed, Ujjayinī became like a desolate wilderness, its streets and marketplaces empty;
it was as Ayodhyā became when Rāma, the delight of all people’s hearts, had gone to heaven and its prosperity was destroyed.
Having gone there, the king gazed upon his son, wept for a long time, and lamented variously with Vilāsavatī;
then, renouncing the splendor of his kingdom like an ascetic, he remained right there, clad in bark garments, even until today.
Having said this and having yawned, the venerable Jābāli paused for a moment and spoke again: "Oh, how long a story has been told out of passion!
That son of Śukanāsa who was cursed by Mahāśvetā—this is he, Vaiśampāyana, who has today attained the state of a parrot through that very deed."
Moreover, that which his father Śukanāsa, provoked by his lack of discipline, said—
"That parrot was taught in vain"— has today borne fruit like a curse.
Having heard this story, the groups of ascetics, filled with wonder, asked again: "O Blessed One, what was the cause that even for this sage, Madaṇa was so great?

Jābāli replied: "Indeed, it has already been stated that he was born solely from the power of a woman; therefore, due to his state of being *rajasvala* (possessing *rajas*), he came to possess the nature of a woman."
When that great seer had finished speaking these words and ceased his speech, the night also reached its end, just as the story had done;
thereupon, the company of sages accomplished their meditative tasks appropriate for the time of the morning twilight.
Thus ends the seventh canto in the *Kādambarī-kathāsāra*, composed by Abhinanda, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Jayanta, who was counted among the foremost of the most excellent and wise teachers.
The Eighth Canto:
Now, [he saw] me, to whom the entire sequence of the narrative as told by Śruta and Jābāli had been related.
Even in his state of childhood, he possessed the recollection of his deeds in previous births.
Having been the son of Śvetaketu, I became the son of Śukanāsa;
indeed, that Vaiśampāyana has now been born as the son of a bird.
As I regained my memory of past lives, my eloquence became manifest;
the sciences of my previous births entered my heart of their own accord.
Just as other past conditioned phenomena have come to me,
so too has my passion for Mahāśvetā arrived.
Then, gradually nourished by the abundant fat of the *hārīta* bird,
I developed my fledgelings and acquired the power to traverse the sky.
Then, as the days passed by, having gradually attained youth,
I desired to go to Mahāśvetā’s hermitage, longing for the sight of her.
And I thought: "May this birth of mine pass away even as a bird dwelling in the hollow of a tree near the hermitage of Mahāśvetā."
Then once, at his father’s command, Kapiñjala went to the hermitage of Jābāli, being entirely under the sway of affection for his friend.
And he asked Hārīta, "Where is Vaiśampāyana Śuka?
To which I replied, "I have recognized him; here I am."
Then, placing me upon his chest, he wept for a long time:
"Alas! Such is the condition of my friend Puṇḍarīka!"
I too spoke to him while weeping: "Why do you weep, Kapiñjala?
Friend, have you also witnessed such a most miserable state on my account?"
Where is the neighing, and where the practice of recitation? Where is the saddle, and where the bark garment? Where is the sacred thread, and where the bridle? Where is the sage, and where the horse?
Then, after remaining still for a moment as it were, Kapiñjala, eager to depart once more, briefly delivered his father’s message.
"Father has commanded you thus; my child, what fault is yours in this?
For those born from the seed of pure women, the transformations of passion are natural."
Although I knew that your life would be short, I did not take any remedial action once you were born; for that was indeed my own laziness.
The sacrifice for the sake of longevity has now been commenced;
it shall be completed, and until it is finished, you must not go anywhere from here.
Although I desired to remain in your presence, I was prevented by my father;
there, I became a mere participant in a tiny fraction of his work.
Having spoken thus and embraced me,
and having taken leave of the sages one by one through the performance of ritual acts, he set out, soaring toward heaven.
Even though I had received my father’s command, in the course of time I was forcibly led by Kāma,
who dragged me under his own sway while holding me back with his left hand.
Having experienced there for a long time various terrifying manifestations of passion,
I formed the resolve to depart, even though it meant transgressing my teacher’s command.
Once, however, seeing the hermitage empty and the ascetics departed,
I suddenly took flight alone and set out toward the northern direction.
Not having yet practiced crossing long distances, I had not flown far when,
overcome by thirst and exhaustion, I looked for water somewhere.
Then, having drunk some water somewhere and having tasted something with my beak, I,
being exhausted, entered the hollow of a certain tree to rest.
Then, as I sat there for a moment, my mind was seized by a deep sleep and my body by a series of snares.
Then, having awakened from sleep, I saw before me, not very far away,
a young elephant as if its purpose were fulfilled, [freed] from my bonds.
From his appearance and his actions, and by his capacity as well as his desire for flesh,
I spoke something tender with my request for the sake of my own liberation.
O noble one, you indeed have a gentle appearance; you do not seem like one seeking meat.
For it is not fitting for those seeking meat to wait for the interruption of sleep.
Therefore, let the Noble One release me, so that I may go wherever I desire in peace.
What purpose do you have by my being bound, or what loss do you suffer by my being released?
He said: "O parrot, you were not captured by me independently;
for you were well known as belonging to Jālābha and had resided in his hermitage for a very long time."
Since you have come within the hearing of my mistress’s daughter, you have been seized by her command;
how can you be released by me?
Furthermore, O gentle one, you are a youth; you do not know this state called the pain of love. You ought not to restrain me, who am drawn away by longing for my beloved.
He replied: "The command of a master must not be transgressed even by a young servant;
how then could I venture to abandon you?"
The sage, who had regained his memory of former births through the curse, spoke to him again:
"I have become a female parrot; release me, and you shall attain supreme merit."
He said to him: "I do not know whether you are a sage, a gandharva, a rākṣasa, or a piśāca; you have simply been brought to the marketplace."
Having said this, he took me by the hand and led me by force to the hamlet;
and he made me enter the wretched dwelling of a Caṇḍāla maiden.
Then, seeing that [corpse] thick with the mire of raw beef, fat, and blood,
and bristling with wriggling worms, it seemed as if my own wretched life-breaths had departed.
Then he presented me to the daughter of the Mātaṅga, saying,
"Mistress, this is that Śuka Vaiśampāyana who was brought here."
Gazing at me as if with a hidden intention, her eyes moist with tears of affection,
she held me to her breast for a moment and then cast me into my cage.
Then, an exceedingly great sorrow took root in my heart:
"Having been a sage, I have now become a pet parrot for a Caṇḍālī. (AK 8.39)
"Alas! By Jābāli, who possesses divine vision, a great wrong has been done to me—he who made his speech explicit and reminded me of my own birth. (AK 8.40)
"Alas! A great and unbearable hardship has arrived;
I, a brahmin, must spend my time in the house of a caṇḍāla."
"Let it be; by fasting alone I shall abandon this wretched life.
Even when being beaten, I will not eat, nor will I utter a word."
Thus, if she is made to feel revulsion, she might either kill me or abandon me;
in either case, this path is for my own welfare.
Thus, as my resolve was fully formed, this daughter of a Caṇḍāla, having brought me fruit and water, spoke to me with a sweet voice: AK 8.44.
"Eat the fruits, drink the water; why do you look about?
Even though you have broken your vow of silence, why do you maintain silence today? (AK 8.45)
O Sage, even if you possess the memory of your past lives, nevertheless,
today your very means of subsistence remains appropriate for one born as an animal.
For those who know the treatises understand that a treatise does not have animals as its intended audience;
for where are the purificatory rites such as the tonsure and the initiation ceremony for animals?
If you intend today to deliberate upon what may and may not be eaten,
why then have you not also adopted the rules for purification from the remains of food in this stage of life?
In times of distress, there is nothing that even the twice-born may not eat;
Viśvāmitra took a dog's haunch from our own hand.
"Though you have fasted for two or three days, my child, you appear as if you were longing for death; do not do this, eat some fruit and water."
With these words, which were unlike those of an outcaste and were not suited for women, I was filled with wonder and reflected thus for a long time: AK 8.51.
Surely this woman is not a Caṇḍālī; I think she has attained this state through some deed of her own, or perhaps for my sake alone.
She carries [me] upon her breast like a mother and looks upon me with an affectionate gaze;
she speaks thus, and therefore I shall carry out her excellent word.
Thinking thus, I uttered a word and became intent on food;
and she fed me day after day like a mother.
Day after day I made supplication to fully understand her true nature; yet, even though she was thus entreated, she did not reveal her own form.
Constantly apprehensive of some deity, I spent my time there in that hamlet, being supported by her.
And once, at the end of the third watch of the night, having been abandoned by sleep,
I saw an entire hamlet filled with people who were for the most part noble.
And you shall see yourself described as being within a magnificent new golden cage,
and this maiden exactly as she was seen by the King.
"O King, I do not know that pair, nor who I am, how long I was protected there by her, or for what reason I have been brought here."
Having heard this story described by Vaiśampāyana,
King Śūdraka emerged from his bedchamber and went into the courtyard.
And having gone out in haste, he quickly had that Mātaṅga maiden— who had been seen on the occasion of the court assembly— brought back again.
Then, having entered with her expansive radiance as if bestowing the moonlight of the autumnal moon upon the quarters of the sky,
she began to speak in a voice that surpassed the sound of the lute and broke through the resonance of the flute.
O beloved of Rohiṇī, abode of all arts, lord of the stars, ruler of the night, treasury of nectar—
may I remember the moon, my very self surrendered with its body, as it is bound in affection for the qualities of the essence of Kādambarī.
"Know me, O moon-crested one, to be Śrī, the mother of this evil-minded one;
therefore, may you understand his former conduct—this is why I have brought him into your presence."
This [son] also, having transgressed the teacher’s instruction, his mind enslaved by passion and desiring to depart,
was then observed by his father— who feared his lack of discipline— with an unerring yogic vision.

By his command alone, and in order to experience the imminent ripening of my transgression of the Guru’s instruction, I descended here into this forest; out of fear of contact with people, I have remained there assuming the guise of a Mātaṅga woman.
Restraining him with nooses as he went, she caused him to experience intense sufferings,
while for a long time she awaited the end of your curse and the completion of the sacrifice.
The sage’s sacrifice has reached its final purificatory bath, and his father’s rite has been successfully completed; you too, having remembered your own body, have now fulfilled his command.
Therefore, both of you, freed from the connection with such a defiled body, may now experience union with your beloveds in your own natural forms.

Having spoken thus aloud, that one of divine splendor flew swiftly toward the sky; with flower petals loosened from their garlands by the impetuosity of his departure, he seemed to worship the earth, and with the sounds arising from his moving girdle and anklets, he seemed to bid farewell to the circle of the quarters.
Beholding her as she leapt into the sky, eclipsing the moonlight with the radiance of her own body,
all the people, their eyes fixed upward for a long time, were struck with an indescribable wonder.
Then, in the heart of King Śūdraka, passion— its continuity of virtues such as fortitude cast aside,
having found an opening through the persistent recollection of Kādambarī— began to swell.
He did not hold royal fortune in high regard, nor the earth, nor fame, nor even Sarasvatī;
intoxicated as it were by that very flavor, he remained inwardly and utterly devoted to Kādambarī alone.
Averse to the pleasures of touch and taste, he did not lend his ears even to sweet sounds;
with his eyes fixed on an invisible object, he gradually reached a state where the functions of all his senses were void.
The dull-witted one did not accept the teacher’s instruction, nor did he understand the reality;
he did not strive for its realization, nor was he even able to make an effort.

As if overcome by a spirit, as if bewildered, the king was gradually brought to a state of unconsciousness by the agony of separation; after enduring the affliction of love for a very long time, he suddenly gave up his life, and the bird did likewise.
When the vital essence and the lunar radiance had established their seat within his body, that very same [essence] then transferred to another body;
for the transformations of the universal nature are indeed wondrous.

In the meantime, as she remained on the banks of the Ācchodā river engaged in asceticism, a very long period of time passed for the daughter of Citraratha, who daily worshipped the body of her beloved.
Then, when the spring season had blossomed, on the day of the great festival of Love,
she adorned her body exceedingly with saffron, sandalwood paste, musk, necklaces, and flowers for her husband.
Beholding him, even though she appeared like an ascetic, she then fell within the range of the god of love who had blossomed with spring;
casting her eyes alone toward the quarters of the sky, she embraced her beloved, who was as if sleeping soundly, with great intensity.
And she embraced Candrāpīḍa firmly by the neck and regained her life;
through that, she attained an unprecedented splendor of joy, like the shore of the ocean touched by the moon.
Having left his bed of stone, and having stood for a moment as if just awakened from a long sleep, Candrāpīḍa opened his eyes with a face languid from yawning;
then, with a voice as resonant as the sound of a beaten drum, he spoke sweetly with a smile to his beloved.
O slender-limbed one, you have secured a birth in the lineage of the Apsarases, which is the source of nectar;
for by this mere fragment of an embrace from you, this person has suddenly regained his life.
This curse, like a second stain that robs one of luster, has brought me to this state;
O ascetic, O slender-limbed one, it was caused solely by separation from you, and it has even led to the death of Śūdraka’s body.
"O slender-waisted one, the curse that 'this body of yours shall be cherished as dear' has come to an end;
for from this day forward, rule over the entire world of the moon and this world marked by the seal of your feet."

Behold Puṇḍarīka, whose splendor is unimpaired and whose cheeks are slightly pale, as he descends from the realm of the moon; his lotus-hands are placed in the hands of Kapiñjala, who has attained divine life through the penances of his father for the sake of his friend’s beloved.
Out of curiosity, you may at some point go with me to the world of the moon to behold Pattralekhā;
she is a certain dear companion of mine. Therefore, let there be no grief for you today arising from not having obtained her.

Having heard these words of his, Kādambarī became filled with longing; wearing a natural mantle of horripilation, her beauty of eyes sprinkled with droplets of tears of joy, she fell at the feet of her husband.
Rising and hastening toward Mahāśvetā, she embraced her and, having made her witness to the path of Puṇḍarīka and having caused her to attain a festival of joy,

she impetuously summoned Keyūraka to announce that by good fortune [Puṇḍarīka] had increased their prosperity, and dispatched the attendants to Tārāpīḍa’s penance grove and others to the house of his parents.
Tārāpīḍa, though emaciated and wasted, arrived there quickly, followed by his joyful harem, attendants, and circle of ministers;
at that time, Puṇḍarīka also, accompanied by his friend, approached his beloved from the sky with his face slightly bowed in shame.
Then Candrāpīḍa, though knowing his own form [as the same person], bowed to Tārāpīḍa as if he were his son;
likewise, being of a humble nature and filled with joy, he saluted Śukanāsa and all his mothers.
Is this an illusion of the Blessed One, or is it the power of Śvetaketu’s asceticisms, or perhaps a magical conjuration by the moon?
Vaiśampāyana was thus made known; for though he was alone, he was surrounded by his kinsmen, and Puṇḍarīka remained present there with them.
That sage Puṇḍarīka also beheld his own son Śukanāsa within;
having prostrated on the ground before his father, he then in due order paid homage to his mothers, Manoramā and the others.
Then Vilāsavatī, together with Samanoramā, whose breasts were dripping with strings of milk drops,
experienced the great festival of embracing her son’s body, whereby all her desires bore fruit.

But Tārāpīḍa, with tears of joy flowing incessantly from his eyes, somehow raised up the prostrate Candrāpīḍa with both arms, embraced him around the neck, and said, "Even if you have descended here due to a curse, you are nonetheless the supreme guardian of the world"; having thus spoken, he, with his body bowed low, worshipped his feet.
Having offered the circle of kings to him with effort, even though he was unwilling, and accompanied by the royal fortune that had come to him in due course,
he did not abandon his long-accumulated hermitage, even when entreated by them along with his queen, for the sake of the fourth [ashrama].

There arrived the lords of kings, radiant with heads adorned by the luster of brilliant gems set in their crests, greyed by the dust kicked up by the hooves of galloping horses; their lotus-eyes wide and trembling with the impatience of beholding Candrāpīḍa like the moon, they had prepared unsurpassed offerings out of sincere eagerness.

Then Citraratha, together with Madirā, and Haṃsa, along with Gaurī, arrived at the earth— which seemed as if it had resolved to take the form of a dance— to witness the rhythmic clapping of hands performed by throngs of Gandharva maidens, who were trembling with excitement from the joy of obtaining more than they had intended.

Having approached them, the two of them cast off the appearance of ascetics for the sake of their daughters; when the wedding festival had been completed—with its daughter-in-law attired in a captivating dress adorned with radiant auspicious ornaments, and its commencement made beautiful by the performance of mantras and fire-offerings—all present, delighted by their mutual reunion, attained great joy.
Thus, with his playful charms fully displayed, sporting in various garden pastimes in both heaven and on earth together with Puṇḍarīka,
and his joy increasing through the attainment of all desired fruits, the moon in the form of Candrāpīḍa attained supreme glory.
Thus ends the eighth canto in the *Kādambarī-kathāsāra*, the work of Abhinanda, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Jayanta, sovereign of all learned men.
